terms.definition: One vertex of a parsed syntax tree: a typed span of source with its children.
A region of code that owns names: a corpus, realm, package, module, class or callable; one node of the tree slop carves the sources into.
A declared type whose instances share fields and methods.
A check that compares one measure of a scope with a stated limit and reports a violation when the measure crosses it.
The facts slop knows about one language: which syntax nodes are callables, classes, decisions and imports, and how names bind.
A callable declared in a class and called on its instances.
A read-only computation over a scope, such as its structure or its lexicon.
A function, method or lambda: a scope that runs when called.
A statement that makes another module, or names from it, available in this one.
One source file, or in Go the files sharing one package declaration.
The whole body of source slop analyses in one run: the root of the ownership tree.
A value written directly in source: a number, string or boolean.
The value a rule allows its measure to reach; crossing it is a violation.
A project's settings for slop: which rules run and their limits.
A programming language slop parses with one grammar.
The name a method uses for its own instance: self, this, or a Go receiver.
A directory of modules that its language treats as one unit.
A number computed from a scope's syntax, such as complexity, coupling or volume.
What a name occurrence refers to: a parameter, local, import, field, method, or nothing in its file.
The words the code declares, split from its identifiers and counted by stem.
The words a project agrees on, what each means, and how they relate: the project's ontology file.
The part of a corpus written in one language.
A rule's report that a scope crossed a limit, at a source location.
A method whose only statement returns one instance member or assigns a plain value to one: a getter or setter.
